content:
Compare accommodation by the whole contract, not just the weekly rent. Look at bills, deposits, guarantor requirements, travel time and the dates you will need the room.

What students actually pay in 2026

The 2026 National Student Accommodation Survey puts average student rent at £575 a month, with sharp regional spread: £793 in London, £703 in Scotland, £492 in the North West and £475 in Wales. Students living at home pay the least, around £400, and the survey found parents contribute an average of £205 a month towards rent. Whatever housing type you choose, the checked-visa figure of £1,171 outside London is close to what students actually spend, while London's £1,529 rate leaves a thinner margin against the £793 average rent.

Contract differences matter as much as headline rent. University halls usually include bills and a nine-to-twelve month contract; private student accommodation charges per room with similar inclusions but higher prices; shared private rentals are cheaper per person but add bills and council-tax handling; homestays bundle meals and utilities into one figure. Compare total monthly cost — rent plus bills plus transport — before comparing cities.

[[chart:rent-regions]][[chart:rent-vs-maintenance]]

Contract terms that cost more than rent

The monthly figure on a listing is the floor, not the price. Length first: many private halls quote a 51-week contract while term-time only runs 39, so a cheaper weekly rate can still cost more across the year - divide the annual total by twelve before comparing. Bills next: in halls and most purpose-built blocks, utilities and internet are included, while a shared private rental adds 60 to 100 pounds a month per person and hands you the council-tax question, which full-time students normally escape but mixed households do not. Deposits in England are capped at five weeks' rent and must be protected in a government-approved scheme within 30 days.

Homestays price differently. Because meals and utilities are bundled, a 600 to 800 pound homestay can undercut central halls once feeding yourself is counted, and the cultural immersion is real; the trade-off is house rules and commute time. Whatever the type, ask for the total annual cost in writing - rent, bills, cleaning, insurance and the deposit - and compare that number against the 575-pound UK average and 793-pound London average from the 2026 survey.

Compare the whole contract

A room's weekly price is only one part of the cost. Check the contract length, included bills, deposit, payment schedule and cancellation conditions. For research students, a short teaching-year contract may leave a gap when you still need to be near the university.

University halls

Halls can simplify moving because the university provides a defined application process and accommodation information. Check eligibility for postgraduate students, room types and the actual location. A place is not guaranteed unless the university's terms say it is, and some rooms may have shared facilities or restrictions relevant to your needs.

Private student accommodation

Purpose-built student housing often offers a clear room package, but compare charges and contract dates carefully. Ask about the guarantor, payment requirements and what happens if your visa or admission arrangements change. An attractive photograph is not evidence that the room suits your budget or travel needs.

Private rentals and shared housing

Check who manages the property, which costs are included and what documents you must provide. Consider transport, working space and noise alongside price. Read the agreement and use the university's accommodation team or a reputable advice service if terms are unclear.

Homestays

A homestay may offer a different living environment, but arrangements vary. Ask about meals, access to facilities, house rules, guests, study space and distance from campus. Confirm the payment and cancellation terms before treating it as a flexible short-term option.

Before paying

Verify the property and the person or organisation offering it. Keep written records and follow the university's advice on avoiding accommodation fraud. Budget for any deposit and the cost of temporary housing while you search.

Use current local prices rather than a generic forecast for a future year. Make a shortlist showing total contract cost and the practical trade-offs; that gives you a clearer decision than comparing headline weekly rent alone.

Read the contract dates before the room photos

Check when the tenancy begins and ends, whether bills are included and what happens if your arrival is delayed. Ask about deposits, guarantors and cancellation terms before paying. For research students, a short teaching-term contract may not cover the period you need to work on campus. Compare the commute and access to a quiet workspace as well as price. If you cannot inspect the property yourself, use the university’s accommodation advice and verification process. Attractive photos are not evidence that an advert or payment request is genuine.

Compare total cost over the dates you need

A weekly rent is only meaningful alongside the length of the contract and included services. For a research degree, check whether you need the room throughout the year. A cheaper term-time room may require a move, storage and temporary housing when the contract ends. Put those costs beside the annual total rather than comparing only the displayed weekly price.

For illustration, a room at £180 for fifty-one weeks costs £9,180. A room at £200 for forty-four weeks costs £8,800 before any extra accommodation needed outside that contract. These are invented prices to explain the arithmetic, not current market rates. Add bills, transport and mandatory charges before deciding which option fits your actual dates.

Questions for each housing type

OptionUseful feature to investigateContract question
University-managed housingArrival support and proximity to university servicesWho is eligible, and what dates are guaranteed?
Private student residenceIncluded services and room typeAre bills capped, and what additional charges apply?
Shared private rentalHousehold size and location flexibilityIs liability individual or shared, and what does the tenancy require?
HomestayHousehold arrangements and included meals or servicesWhat rules, access arrangements and cancellation terms apply?

None of these options is automatically cheaper or more suitable. Consider privacy, accessibility, commuting, household preferences and whether dependants can live there. Ask about the specific property rather than relying on the general category.

Before transferring a deposit

Verify the property, provider and payment instructions. Use the university accommodation service for guidance on unfamiliar contracts and potential scams. Be careful with urgent requests to pay a personal account before you have seen a proper agreement. If you cannot visit, ask about an authorised viewing or another verification method recommended by the housing service.

Read the cancellation clause and ask what happens if a visa is delayed or refused. A verbal promise of flexibility may not appear in the agreement. Retain the written terms and payment confirmation. Rules on deposits, tenancy arrangements and charges can differ across the UK's nations, so use guidance relevant to the property's location.

Check the room as a place to live and work

Research can involve irregular hours, remote meetings or writing at home. Ask about internet access, desk space, noise and transport after evening work. Check accessibility needs directly and early. If a room is described as accessible, ask which features are actually provided rather than inferring that it meets every requirement.

Should I choose the lowest weekly rent?

Compare the whole contract, bills and commuting costs first. The lowest weekly price can become more expensive if it leaves gaps in accommodation or requires substantial additional travel.

Can a university guarantee housing?

Only rely on the guarantee or offer that the university actually provides for your applicant category and dates. An accommodation information page is not the same as a reserved room.

Ask about moving in and moving out

Check key collection, arrival hours and the inventory process before travelling. On arrival, follow the provider's instructions for recording the room's condition and report discrepancies promptly. Before the contract ends, read the notice, cleaning and key-return requirements. Keep records of payments and correspondence. These details help prevent a low advertised rent from distracting you from obligations elsewhere in the agreement.

Questions applicants often ask

How much is student accommodation in the UK in 2026?

The UK average is £575 a month, rising to £793 in London and £703 in Scotland, according to Save the Student's 2026 survey. Wales is the cheapest region at £475.

Do halls include bills?

University halls and most private student blocks include utilities, internet and insurance in the rent. Shared private rentals usually exclude bills, so add roughly £60–£100 a month per person before comparing prices.
